The **2024 Copa América final** was an international [soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") match to determine the winners of the [CONMEBOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CONMEBOL "CONMEBOL") [2024 Copa América](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Copa_América "2024 Copa América"). The match was played at [Hard Rock Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_Rock_Stadium "Hard Rock Stadium") in [Miami Gardens, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Gardens,_Florida "Miami Gardens, Florida"), on July 14, 2024.[[5]](#cite_note-5) Kickoff was delayed by over an hour and twenty minutes due to overcrowding and other incidents which occurred near the stadium.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-finals-match-delayed-7)

The match was [Argentina's eighth final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina_at_the_Copa_América "Argentina at the Copa América"), further extending its record, and was Colombia's third Copa América final. Before the match, Argentina had won a joint-record 15 titles; 12 won with a round-robin format and three by winning finals, and Colombia's most recent final win was in [2001](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Copa_América "2001 Copa América").

Defending champions [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina_national_football_team "Argentina national football team") defeated [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia_national_football_team "Colombia national football team") 1–0 after extra time to claim a record-breaking 16th Copa América title.[[8]](#cite_note-Athletic-result-8) It was also Argentina's third consecutive major tournament triumph, following successes at the [2021 Copa América](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Copa_América "2021 Copa América") in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") and the [2022 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_FIFA_World_Cup "2022 FIFA World Cup") in [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar"), a streak previously only achieved by [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_national_football_team "Spain national football team") ([2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2008 "UEFA Euro 2008"), [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_FIFA_World_Cup "2010 FIFA World Cup"), and [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2012 "UEFA Euro 2012")) and themselves ([1945](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1945_South_American_Championship "1945 South American Championship"), [1946](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1946_South_American_Championship "1946 South American Championship"), and [1947](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1947_South_American_Championship "1947 South American Championship")).[[9]](#cite_note-9)

## Venue

[Hard Rock Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_Rock_Stadium "Hard Rock Stadium") in [Miami Gardens, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Gardens,_Florida "Miami Gardens, Florida"), near the city of [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami "Miami"), hosted the final. It was confirmed as the host on November 20, 2023.[[10]](#cite_note-Herald-Host-10) The United States had been announced as host in January 2023; the country had previously hosted the [Copa América Centenario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_América_Centenario "Copa América Centenario") in 2016 with the [final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_América_Centenario_final "Copa América Centenario final") played at [MetLife Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetLife_Stadium "MetLife Stadium") in [East Rutherford, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Rutherford,_New_Jersey "East Rutherford, New Jersey"), near [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), which would also host the [2025 FIFA Club World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_FIFA_Club_World_Cup "2025 FIFA Club World Cup") final and the [2026 FIFA World Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_FIFA_World_Cup_final "2026 FIFA World Cup final").[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12)

Hard Rock Stadium is primarily the home of the [Miami Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Dolphins "Miami Dolphins") of the [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") and has a grass surface and 65,000 seats.[[13]](#cite_note-NBC-Stadium-13) It opened in 1987 and underwent major renovations from 2015 to 2017 that added a roof and other features.[[14]](#cite_note-14) The stadium is also a [2026 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_FIFA_World_Cup "2026 FIFA World Cup") host venue.[[13]](#cite_note-NBC-Stadium-13)

## Entertainment

![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/2023-11-16_Gala_de_los_Latin_Grammy%2C_03_%28cropped%2902.jpg/250px-2023-11-16_Gala_de_los_Latin_Grammy%2C_03_%28cropped%2902.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

### National anthems

Before the final, Colombian singer [Karol G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_G "Karol G") and Argentine singer [Abel Pintos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Pintos "Abel Pintos") sang the national anthems of their respective countries.[[15]](#cite_note-26_minutes-15)

### Half-time show

[Shakira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakira "Shakira") was announced to perform at the [halftime show of the final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Copa_América_final_halftime_show "2024 Copa América final halftime show") on July 8, 2024.[[16]](#cite_note-16) She performed four songs with backup dancers and robots.[[15]](#cite_note-26_minutes-15)[[17]](#cite_note-17) The extension of halftime from the traditional 15 minutes to 26 minutes was criticized by Colombia coach [Néstor Lorenzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Néstor_Lorenzo "Néstor Lorenzo") prior to the match.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

**Copa América**, [South America](https://www.britannica.com/place/South-America)’s premier men’s [football (soccer)](https://www.britannica.com/sports/football-soccer) tournament. The Copa América is held every four years and is the world’s oldest international football tournament. The tournament is governed by the [Confederación Sudamericana de Fútbol](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Confederacion-Sudamericana-de-Futbol) (CONMEBOL; South American Football Federation) and features CONMEBOL’s 10 member countries—[Argentina](https://www.britannica.com/place/Argentina), [Bolivia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Bolivia), [Brazil](https://www.britannica.com/place/Brazil), [Chile](https://www.britannica.com/place/Chile), [Colombia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Colombia), [Ecuador](https://www.britannica.com/place/Ecuador), [Paraguay](https://www.britannica.com/place/Paraguay), [Peru](https://www.britannica.com/place/Peru), [Uruguay](https://www.britannica.com/place/Uruguay), and [Venezuela](https://www.britannica.com/place/Venezuela)—along with two invited national teams from outside the continent. The championship has featured popular footballers such as [Pelé](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Pele-Brazilian-football-player), [Diego Maradona](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Diego-Maradona), Zico, [Gabriel Batistuta](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gabriel-Batistuta), [Ronaldo](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ronaldo), Luis Suárez, [Lionel Messi](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lionel-Messi), and [Neymar](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Neymar).

## History

Did You Know?

The Copa América Femenina is South America’s premier women’s football tournament, organized by CONMEBOL. First held in 1991, the tournament not only [crowns](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/crowns) the continental champion but also serves as a qualifier for the [FIFA Women’s World Cup](https://www.britannica.com/sports/Womens-World-Cup), [Olympic Games](https://www.britannica.com/sports/Olympic-Games), and [Pan American Sports Games](https://www.britannica.com/sports/Pan-American-Sports-Games). As of 2024 the Brazilian national team has dominated the tournament, winning all editions except in 2006, when Argentina was crowned champion.

The Copa América was first held in 1916 in honor of the 100th anniversary of Argentina’s independence. Uruguay won the inaugural title. It was initially called the South American Football Championship and was renamed the Copa América in 1975. The format of the tournament has evolved over the years and, starting in 1993, national teams from other continents were invited to participate. [Mexico](https://www.britannica.com/place/Mexico) and the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) were the first non-CONMEBOL teams to play in the tournament, with Mexico finishing as [runner-up](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/runner-up) in 1993. The Copa América was held at irregular intervals (annually, biennially, or even after longer gaps) until it adopted a quadrennial format in 2007.

 

In 2016, just a year after the 2015 edition, CONMEBOL held a special tournament called the Copa América Centenario to celebrate 100 years of the Copa América. Hosted by the U.S., it was the first Copa América to be held outside South America. Chile won the 2016 tournament, defeating Argentina in the final. The next regular Copa América was held in 2019, four years after the 2015 edition. CONMEBOL decided to hold the tournament again in 2020 to align it with the UEFA [European Championship](https://www.britannica.com/sports/European-Championship). However, the event was postponed to 2021 because of the outbreak of [COVID-19](https://www.britannica.com/science/COVID-19). The 2024 edition was also held in the U.S.
